summary: A request from the University of Utah for comments on making its Univac 1108 computer, running EXEC 8, available to the ARPANET. Interest had been shown at the ICCC conference, and since the 1108 already talked to the Utah PDP-10, little programming effort would be needed.

eli5.summary: A school asks if people would like to use its other big computer over the network, since it would be easy to connect.

questions: what computing resources did utah offer on the network
what priority system did utah propose for computer access
subtitle: Proposal to share University of Utah's large mainframe computer on the network

tldr.problem: University of Utah had a powerful Univac 1108 mainframe with EXEC 8 system that went underutilized. Connecting it to ARPANET would allow remote users to access it with minimal programming effort.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the 1108's capabilities, peripheral equipment, software libraries, and proposes a pricing schedule and priority system for batch and interactive computing.
tldr.outcome: The RFC sought community feedback on the desirability of the service, with detailed resource descriptions, rate schedules, and time availability.

today: RFC 403 is classified as Unknown status. It represents a historical proposal to share computing resources in 1973.

sections.title: Network Service Proposal
sections.content: The University of Utah proposed making its Univac 1108 computer available to ARPANET users. Interest in this service had been expressed at the recent ICCC conference in Washington. Since the 1108 already communicated with Utah's PDP-10, the RFC argued that minimal programming effort would be needed to enable network access, and seeks community feedback on whether such a service would be desirable.
sections.eli5: Utah has an extra big computer that is not always busy. It could talk to the network with not much work. Should they do it?

sections.title: Computing Facilities
sections.content: The Univac 1108 system featured six tape drives, seven high-speed drums, 262 megabytes of on-line storage, and communication equipment for both slow (teletype) timesharing and high-speed (RJE) batch terminals. The Computer Center operated 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Available software included FORTRAN, COBOL, SNOBOL, APL, BASIC, MAD, ALGOL, LISP, a text editor, and an assembler. A wide variety of scientific and statistical routines and simulation packages were available, with computing rates considerably lower than commercial rates.
sections.eli5: The machine could handle tape backups, store huge amounts of data, and had every programming language available. It was cheap to use.

sections.title: Service Rates and Schedule
sections.content: The RFC included a detailed pricing schedule for CPU time, I/O operations, terminal connection, page printing, card processing, tape mounting, and equipment rental. A priority and rate schedule offered different cents-per-second charges based on priority level (A-F reserved, G-Z for users). Interactive teletype service received priority 6 cents above the lowest priority being accepted at the time. The schedule showed daily and weekly time slots when different priority levels were available, with holidays and weekends having reserved Z-priority times for lower cost.
sections.eli5: Computer time cost between 5 and 45 cents per second depending on how soon you needed your answer. Different times of day had different prices.
